title: Lior and the Winter
premise: In 1996, folklorist Marguerite Galloway returns to Hollowmere to record a carol cycle that no villager will sing twice, only to find her childhood imaginary friend, Lior, waiting on her porch—frozen at nine years old and unchanged since 1974. Lior remembers what the village has paid to forget: something was taken from each household that winter, and the last surviving resident, old Mrs. Vane, is about to sign papers that will erase Hollowmere's memory entirely and free what was buried beneath it. As Marguerite's disbelief erodes and her own identity begins to fray—she discovers she may be one of the taken—Lior must return what was stolen before the ink dries, even if returning it means surrendering his own existence.
about_author: Emrys Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing oral histories in remote English villages before turning to fiction. They write horror rooted in folk tradition, insisting that every ghost story is really a record-keeping error.

chapters.title: The Porch That Waited
chapters.summary: Marguerite arrives in Hollowmere with recording equipment and professional skepticism, finding the village shuttered and hostile. On her rented cottage porch sits a small boy in a 1970s coat who greets her by a childhood nickname. POV: Marguerite. Beat: uncanny recognition she refuses to name.

chapters.title: Songs Sung Once
chapters.summary: Marguerite interviews villagers about the winter carol cycle; each agrees to sing once, then goes pale and refuses repetition. Lior watches from doorways, unnoticed by everyone but her. POV: Marguerite. Beat: mounting dread disguised as fieldwork frustration.

chapters.title: Nine Years Old Forever
chapters.summary: Lior's POV: he explains he woke on the porch when she crossed the parish boundary, unchanged since the night she stopped believing in him. He remembers 1974 in fragments—a bell, a ledger, hands taking things. Beat: tenderness laced with wrongness.

chapters.title: Mrs. Vane's Papers
chapters.summary: Marguerite visits Edith Vane, ninety-one, the last original resident, who is preparing to sign documents selling the village to developers. Vane warns her: 'Don't let them finish the count.' POV: Marguerite. Beat: first explicit threat.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Keeps
chapters.summary: In the church archive, Marguerite finds a 1974 parish ledger listing households beside blank columns labeled 'RECEIVED.' Every column is empty except smudged indentations. Lior can read the impressions by touch. POV: alternating. Beat: discovery that something was collected, not lost.

chapters.title: The Carol That Isn't a Carol
chapters.summary: A drunk pub singer performs half the seventh verse of the winter song before collapsing mid-word. Transcribing it, Marguerite realizes the lyrics are an inventory—a list of names being counted down. POV: Marguerite. Beat: horror through scholarship.

chapters.title: Hollow Places
chapters.summary: Villagers begin forgetting things: spouses' faces, their own trades, the road out. The blanks in their memories match the ledger's empty columns. Lior feels himself growing more solid as they grow less. POV: Lior. Beat: dread of exchange—he exists because they don't.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Missing Year
chapters.summary: Checking her own records, Marguerite finds a gap: no photographs, no school reports between December 1974 and spring 1975. Her mother's letters call her 'our returned girl.' POV: Marguerite. Beat: identity crisis—the folklorist becomes the folklore.

chapters.title: The Bell Under the Hill
chapters.summary: Lior leads Marguerite to the barrow above the village where, in 1974, the parish buried 'the winter's due' beneath a disused chapel bell. Digging is impossible; frost rises from the ground like breath. POV: Lior. Beat: the debt has a location.

chapters.title: Sign Here
chapters.summary: The developer's lawyer arrives; Vane, suddenly lucid and terrified, begs Marguerite to stop the sale but cannot say why. That night every clock in Hollowmere stops at 11:47, the minute of the 1974 collection. POV: Marguerite. Beat: deadline made physical.

chapters.title: Verse Eight
chapters.summary: Marguerite coaxes the full eighth verse from a dying choirmaster: it names the taker—'the Tall Neighbour, who counts what we owe.' He dies before verse nine, mouth still moving. POV: Marguerite. Beat: the antagonist acquires shape.

chapters.title: Lior's First Memory
chapters.summary: Lior recovers his origin: he was not imaginary. He was the Galloway family's payment in 1974—a child-shaped thing left in place of the real Marguerite, discarded when she came home. He has been waiting forty years to give her back. POV: Lior. Beat: devastating loyalty revelation.

chapters.title: Which One of Us Is Real
chapters.summary: Marguerite confronts the possibility that she died or was replaced, that her memories are borrowed. Lior insists she is real—but 'real' in Hollowmere means 'still owed for.' POV: Marguerite. Beat: identity theme at its darkest.

chapters.title: The Counting House
chapters.summary: Following the ledger's logic, they find the old tithe barn converted into a shrine: forty-two objects wrapped in cloth, one per household, each humming the winter song. One bundle bears Marguerite's name. POV: alternating. Beat: rising tension peaks; the stakes are tangible.

chapters.title: Vane Confesses
chapters.summary: Edith Vane admits she was the collector's clerk in 1974; the signing isn't a property sale but a final settlement releasing the Tall Neighbour from its obligations—with nothing returned. She gives Marguerite the clerk's key. POV: Marguerite. Beat: guilt, complicity, a fragile alliance.

chapters.title: Frost Line
chapters.summary: The village freezes inward overnight; roads end in white nothing. The Tall Neighbour walks the lanes, tall and patient, checking bundles against its list. Lior hides Marguerite inside his own memory of her, the one place it cannot look. POV: Lior. Beat: protective love versus annihilation.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: They open the counting house and begin returning the bundles—each object given back unbinds a villager's memory but weakens Lior, who is himself the largest item on the list. POV: alternating. Beat: sacrifice structure established; loyalty vs. truth crystallized.

chapters.title: The Last Bundle
chapters.summary: One bundle remains: Marguerite's own, containing a small cold thing that is unmistakably her. Returning it restores her fully—and unmakes Lior, whose substance was always hers. She hesitates. POV: Marguerite. Beat: the choice the whole book has built toward.

chapters.title: The Signing
chapters.summary: At the solicitor's office, Vane lifts the pen as the Tall Neighbour fills the doorway. Marguerite slams the clerk's key and the restored ledger onto the table: all debts discharged, nothing owed, nothing released. The pen scratches dry. POV: Marguerite. Beat: climax—truth defeats the contract.

chapters.title: Unmade, Unforgotten
chapters.summary: With the count broken, Lior begins to come apart into snowlight. He asks Marguerite to sing the winter song twice—the thing no one would do—for him. She does, all verses, voice breaking. POV: Lior. Beat: grief transfigured into witness.

chapters.title: Spring Audit
chapters.summary: Hollowmere thaws; memories return imperfectly, and the sale collapses. Marguerite archives the complete carol cycle under both their names. On the last page of the ledger, new writing appears: 'PAID IN FULL — L.G.' POV: Marguerite. Beat: mourning with evidence of grace.

chapters.title: Twice-Sung
chapters.summary: Years later, Marguerite teaches the songs to children who sing them willingly, twice over. On a porch in another village, a child tells her about her friend Lior, who waits for someone to believe. She believes. POV: Marguerite. Beat: quiet resolution—memory kept alive is the only true repayment.
